title: Fast Fault-Tolerant Decoders for Hypergraph Product and Lifted-Product Codes
authors: Asit Kumar Pradhan, Nithin Raveendran, David Declercq, Bane Vasić
abstract: We design low-complexity, fault-tolerant decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes with the goal of reducing decoding latency. We target two major bottlenecks of decoding under the \emph{circuit-level} noise model: (i) post-processing via order-statistics decoding (OSD), and (ii) the large number of auxiliary variable nodes commonly introduced to represent CNOT-induced correlations during syndrome extraction. Our key observation is that propagating CNOT faults (\emph{hook errors}) create \emph{stabilizer-induced} trapping sets (TSs) that are intrinsic to hypergraph-product (HGP) and lifted-product (LP) constructions. Therefore, instead of modeling each such fault with an explicit correlation node and relying on OSD to clean up the resulting failures, we design message-passing decoders that resolve the corresponding \emph{stabilizer-induced} TSs directly. We obtain these decoders by deriving QLDPC decoders from decoders for the parent classical LDPC codes and using them collectively to correct broad families of \emph{stabilizer-induced} TSs. For CNOT faults that manifest primarily as syndrome errors, we show that their effect is equivalent to a data error together with syndrome-bit measurement errors. Consequently, given repeated measurements and a decoding graph that already includes nodes representing syndrome-bit errors, no distinct variable node is needed for each CNOT fault. Using a \emph{phenomenological} Tanner graph with nodes representing only data errors and syndrome-bit errors, simulations on the LP codes show a reduction in, or comparable, logical error rates relative to BP+OSD, at substantially lower decoding complexity.
summary: This paper tackles the challenge of developing fast, fault-tolerant decoders for QLDPC codes used in quantum computing. The authors overcome the complexity bottlenecks associated with modeling circuit faults by designing novel message-passing decoders. This results in a decoder that maintains high performance while drastically reducing computational overhead compared to current state-of-the-art methods.
main_problem: The primary goal is to design low-complexity, fault-tolerant decoders for Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (QLDPC) codes to significantly reduce decoding latency.
main_result: The authors propose message-passing decoders that directly resolve stabilizer-induced Trapping Sets (TSs) arising from CNOT faults, achieving error rates comparable to existing methods but with substantially lower decoding complexity.
method: The method involves deriving QLDPC decoders from parent classical LDPC decoders and reinterpreting CNOT faults as a combination of data errors and syndrome-bit measurement errors, thus avoiding explicit fault nodes.
model_or_system: The work focuses on QLDPC codes, specifically those constructed using Hypergraph-Product (HGP) and Lifted-Product (LP) constructions, which are used for quantum error correction.
key_observables: Logical error rates, decoding complexity, and the ability to resolve stabilizer-induced Trapping Sets (TSs).
important_parameters: The structure of the HGP and LP codes, and the nature of the circuit-level noise model (CNOT faults).
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that CNOT faults manifesting as syndrome errors are equivalent to a data error plus syndrome-bit measurement error, allowing for a simplified phenomenological Tanner graph.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes mention illustrating a Tanner graph showing variable and check nodes and constraints.
paper_structure: The paper identifies bottlenecks in existing QLDPC decoding (OSD post-processing and auxiliary nodes for CNOT faults), proposes the key insight regarding stabilizer-induced TSs, and then details the derivation of message-passing decoders to resolve these TSs directly.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of implementing quantum error correction codes by providing a computationally efficient decoding scheme that accounts for realistic circuit noise.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: An example of a Tanner graph. Circular nodes represent variable nodes, and rectangular nodes represent check nodes. Each check node imposes a linear constraint on its neighboring variable nodes. For instance, check node c1 is connected to variable nodes v1 and v2, which implies that in any valid codeword v1 + v2 ≡0 (mod 2).
Fig. 3: Measurement of stabilizers that acts on one qubit.

Fig. 2: Node types in the Tanner graphs of HGP/LP codes. VV-type variable nodes are depicted with a circle inside another circle because they are obtained by multiplying two variable nodes, each represented by a single circle. Analogously, CC-type variable nodes, X-checks, and Z-checks are represented, respectively, by a square inside another square, a circle inside a square, and a square inside a circle.
Fig. 4: Measurement of the Z2Z3Z4Z5 operator.

Fig. 6: Syndrome measurement circuit for the CSS code in 1: The fault locations are shown as a set of random gates Fi, for i ∈[16], which are Pauli matrices with fixed probabilities. The X stabilizer is measured once, and the Z stabilizers are measured twice.
